worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /2$ | $3\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $1+\sqrt{2}$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{u}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{2}-2)\end{aligned}
$$
